steps.body:
If your terms are **smaller** than those of a series you already know converges, yours converges too — it is trapped underneath a finite ceiling.

And if they are **bigger** than those of a known divergent series, yours diverges as well.

That is the comparison test, and it turns every series you know into a **ruler** for measuring new ones.

explanationVariants: The p-series Σ1/nᵖ converges exactly when **p > 1**. So Σ1/n² converges (to π²/6), and Σ1/n — the harmonic — diverges, because p = 1 is not greater than 1.
That single boundary at p = 1 is the most useful fact in the chapter: it is the ruler against which almost everything gets measured.

items.label: Σ 1/n² (p = 2)
items.feedback: p = 2 > 1, so it converges — to π²/6 ≈ 1.645, as it happens.

items.label: Σ 1/n (p = 1)
items.feedback: The harmonic series. p = 1 is NOT greater than 1, and it diverges — the standing counterexample of the chapter.

items.label: Σ 1/√n (p = 1/2)
items.feedback: p = 1/2 < 1, so the terms fade even more slowly than the harmonic's. It diverges too.

items.label: Σ 1/n³ (p = 3)
items.feedback: p = 3 > 1. The bigger p is, the faster the terms fade and the more comfortably it converges.

widget.missFeedback: The whole rule is one boundary: Σ1/nᵖ converges if and only if p > 1.
widget.successFeedback: p > 1 converges; p ≤ 1 diverges. The harmonic series sits exactly on the boundary, on the wrong side of it.

steps.body: Why a smaller pile must be finite.

widget.prompt: The comparison argument, in three moves.

panels.title: Start with a ceiling you trust
panels.body: Σ1/n² converges. Its partial sums pile up and stop, under a ceiling at π²/6 ≈ 1.645. That fact is your ruler.

panels.title: Sit underneath it
panels.body: Every term of Σ1/(n² + 1) is SMALLER than the matching term of Σ1/n². So its partial sums are smaller at every stage — the whole pile sits underneath the other one.

panels.title: So it must stop too
panels.body: A pile of positive terms that is always climbing but never passes 1.645 has nowhere to go but a limit. It converges. Notice you never found out WHAT it converges to — and you never needed to.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the third panel is why the test proves anything at all.
widget.successFeedback: Trapped under a finite ceiling and always climbing: it must settle. The test proves convergence without ever computing the sum.

explanationVariants: 1/(n² + 1) < 1/n² for every n, and Σ1/n² converges. So the smaller series converges too.
Compare term by term with a series you already trust. That is the entire method.

options.label: Yes — each term is smaller than 1/n², and Σ1/n² converges.
options.feedback: Right. Trapped under a convergent pile and always climbing, it has nowhere to go but a limit.

options.label: No — adding 1 to the denominator makes no difference.
options.feedback: It makes the terms SMALLER, which can only help. And Σ1/n² already converges, so the comparison closes the case.

options.label: Yes, because the terms go to zero.
options.feedback: True but not sufficient — the harmonic series has terms going to zero and diverges. The comparison is what does the real work.

options.label: Impossible to say without computing the sum.
options.feedback: You never need the sum. Convergence is about whether a ceiling EXISTS, not about where it is.

steps.body:
The comparison must go the **right way**.

To prove **convergence**, sit under something convergent.
To prove **divergence**, sit above something divergent.

A series smaller than a divergent one proves nothing at all — Σ1/n² is smaller than Σ1/n, and one converges while the other does not.

explanationVariants: Being SMALLER than a divergent series is no help: Σ1/n² is smaller than the divergent Σ1/n, and it converges perfectly well.
The inequality has to point the same way as the conclusion you want.

widget.prompt: A student says: 'Σ1/n² is smaller than the divergent Σ1/n, so it must diverge too.' What is wrong?

options.label: Being smaller than a divergent series proves nothing — Σ1/n² is smaller, and it converges.
options.feedback: Right. Comparison only works in the direction that matches your conclusion: under a convergent ceiling, or over a divergent floor.

options.label: Σ1/n does not actually diverge.
options.feedback: It does — the harmonic series is the standing counterexample of the chapter. The error is the DIRECTION of the comparison.

options.label: The terms are not positive.
options.feedback: Both series have entirely positive terms. That is not the problem.

options.label: Nothing is wrong.
options.feedback: Σ1/n² converges to π²/6, so the conclusion is simply false. The reasoning ran the wrong way.

hints: Compare Σ 1/(n − 1) (from n = 2 onward) with the harmonic series Σ1/n.
For n ≥ 2, is 1/(n − 1) bigger or smaller than 1/n? A smaller denominator makes a BIGGER fraction.
So each term is bigger than the matching harmonic term — and the harmonic diverges.
explanationVariants: 1/(n − 1) > 1/n, and Σ1/n diverges. Sitting ABOVE a divergent series means diverging too.
The direction is what matters: above a divergent floor, you cannot settle.

widget.prompt: Does Σ 1/(n − 1), from n = 2 onward, converge?

options.label: No — each term is BIGGER than 1/n, and the harmonic series diverges.
options.feedback: Right: sitting above a divergent floor, the pile can never settle. (It is the harmonic series in disguise, shifted by one.)

options.label: Yes — the terms go to zero.
options.feedback: So do the harmonic's, and it diverges. Fading terms are necessary, never sufficient.

options.label: Yes, by comparison with Σ1/n².
options.feedback: These terms are far BIGGER than 1/n², so that comparison points the wrong way and proves nothing.

options.label: Impossible to decide.
options.feedback: One comparison settles it: 1/(n − 1) > 1/n, and Σ1/n diverges.

steps.body: Every known series is a ruler.
takeaways: Σ1/nᵖ converges exactly when p > 1. The harmonic series sits ON the boundary, on the wrong side.
To prove convergence, sit UNDER something convergent. To prove divergence, sit OVER something divergent.
A comparison pointing the wrong way proves nothing at all — and you never need to know the actual sum.
steps.teaser: Next: a series that converges only because its terms keep changing their minds.

concept.body: Find a series you already know. If your terms are SMALLER than a convergent one, you converge. If they are BIGGER than a divergent one, you diverge. Any other combination tells you nothing — the inequality has to point the same way as your conclusion.

explanationVariants: Smaller than a CONVERGENT series proves convergence.
Smaller than a divergent one proves nothing at all.

widget.prompt: Your terms are smaller than those of a convergent series. What follows?

options.label: Yours converges too.
options.feedback: Right — trapped under a finite ceiling, and always climbing.

options.label: Nothing follows.
options.feedback: Something does: a positive pile that always climbs and never passes a finite ceiling has to settle.
